title: Count Complete Subarrays
description:
# Count Complete Subarrays

You are given an integer array `nums`.

A subarray is complete if it contains every distinct value that appears anywhere in the whole array `nums` at least once.

Return the number of complete subarrays.

The empty array has no subarrays, so its answer is `0`.

## Example 1:

**Input:** nums = [1,3,1,2,2]
**Output:** 4
**Explanation:** The complete subarrays are `[1,3,1,2]`, `[1,3,1,2,2]`, `[3,1,2]`, and `[3,1,2,2]`.

## Example 2:

**Input:** nums = [5,5,5,5]
**Output:** 10
**Explanation:** The whole array has one distinct value, so every non-empty subarray is complete.

## Example 3:

**Input:** nums = [1,2,3]
**Output:** 1
**Explanation:** Every value is distinct, so only the whole array contains all distinct values.

## Constraints:

* `0 <= nums.length <= 1000`
* `1 <= nums[i] <= 2000`

solutions.name: HashMap Sliding Window
solutions.description:
## Approach

First count how many distinct values appear in the whole array. Then move a right pointer across the array while a frequency map tracks the current window. Whenever the window contains all required distinct values, every subarray with the same left endpoint and any farther right endpoint is complete, so add `nums.length - right` and shrink from the left.

## Key Insight

Completeness is monotonic with respect to extending the right endpoint: once a window `[left, right]` contains every distinct value, `[left, right + 1]`, `[left, right + 2]`, and all later extensions also remain complete. That lets one window event count many subarrays at once.

## Complexity Analysis

Each index enters and leaves the sliding window at most once. The time complexity is O(n), and the frequency map stores at most the number of distinct values, which is O(n) in the worst case.

solutions.name: Enumerate Subarrays Baseline
solutions.description:
## Approach

Compute the global number of distinct values, then enumerate every start index. Extend the end index one step at a time while a set records which values are inside the current subarray. Every time the set size reaches the global distinct count, count that subarray.

## Key Insight

This route mirrors the definition directly, so it is a useful correctness baseline. It also shows why the optimized sliding-window version is allowed to batch-count later endings: this baseline would count those complete endings one by one.

## Complexity Analysis

There are O(n^2) start/end pairs, and each extension updates a set in expected O(1) time. The time complexity is O(n^2), and the set uses O(n) space in the worst case.

solutions.name: Frequency Array Sliding Window
solutions.description:
## Approach

Use the value bound `1 <= nums[i] <= 2000` to replace hash tables with arrays. A boolean array counts the total distinct values in `nums`; a frequency array maintains the sliding window and the number of distinct values currently inside it.

## Key Insight

This is the same monotonic-window idea as the HashMap route, but the bounded value domain makes frequency updates deterministic and compact. It is useful when the value range is small compared with object-heavy hash table overhead.

## Complexity Analysis

Let `V` be the value domain size, here `2000`. Initializing and scanning take O(n + V) time, and the frequency arrays use O(V) space.
